title: Take-home Exercise 01
text:
2 Overview
This take-home exercise investigates the spatial and/or spatio-temporal patterns of public-safety point events using road traffic accidents within the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area.
The object of the exercise are:

To prepare and integrate real-world geospatial and temporal data for spatial and spatio-temporal point-pattern analysis.
To investigate first-order properties of the point pattern by examining how the intensity or distribution of events varies across space and/or time.
To investigate second-order properties by examining whether events exhibit evidence of spatial or spatio-temporal interaction, such as clustering, inhibition, or approximate randomness.
To critically evaluate the analytical assumptions, methodological choices, and limitations associated with the selected point-pattern methods.
To communicate the analytical findings effectively through appropriate geovisualisation and geocommunication.
To translate the analytical evidence into meaningful implications for public-safety planning and management.

3 The data
The following 3 datasets will be used in this exercise.



Dataset Name
Description
Format
Source




Thailand Road Accident [2019-2022]
Data on road accidents in Thailand, including details on location, severity, and date of incidents.
CSV
Kaggle


Thailand Roads (OpenStreetMap Export)
OpenStreetMap Geospatial data of Thailand.
ESRI Shapefile
Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX)


Thailand - Subnational Administrative Boundaries
Boundaries of Thailand’s Geospatial dataset.
ESRI Shapefile
Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX)



About Thailand Road Accident dataset
This dataset provides comprehensive statistics on recorded road accidents in Thailand, spanning from approximately 2019 to 2022. The data was sourced from raw information provided by the Office of the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Transport, which is also utilized in this public dashboard for easier access and visualization. The dataset encompasses various aspects of road accidents and aims to shed light on the trends and patterns within this critical area of concern, analysis of this data could be crucial in guiding road safety policies and measures.







Column
Description




acc_code
The accident code or identifier.


incident_datetime
The date and time of the accident occurrence.


report_datetime
The date and time when the accident was reported.


province_th
The name of the province in Thailand, written in Thai.


province_en
The name of the province in Thailand, written in English.


agency
The government agency responsible for the road and traffic management.


route
The route or road segment where the accident occurred.


vehicle_type
The type of vehicle involved in the accident.


presumed_cause
The presumed cause or reason for the accident.


accident_type
The type or nature of the accident.


number_of_vehicles_involved
The number of vehicles involved in the accident.


number_of_fatalities
The number of fatalities resulting from the accident.


number_of_injuries
The number of injuries resulting from the accident.


weather_condition
The weather condition at the time of the accident.


latitude
The latitude coordinate of the accident location.


longitude
The longitude coordinate of the accident location.


road_description
The description of the road type or configuration where the accident occurred.


slope_description
The description of the slope condition at the accident location.



The original data has total 81735 accident records in all over Thailand from 2019-2022.

Noteset reproducibility value



In order to ensures that stochastic algorithms and randomized spatial processes yield identical results every time the workflow runs, we need to set reproducibility value.



set.seed(1234)

Import road traffic accident data
Loading Thailand road traffic accidents 2019-2022.

bmr_acc <- read_csv(
  "data/thai_road_accident_2019_2022.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Checking for missing values

null_counts <-   sum(is.na(bmr_acc))
null_counts

[1] 718
The dataset contains 718 missing values in total. We will check for missing values in each column to identify which columns have missing data. Listing the number of missing values for each column in the dataset

data.frame(
  Column = colnames(bmr_acc),
  Missing_Values = colSums(is.na(bmr_acc))
)

There are 359 missing values in the latitude column and 359 missing values in the longitude column. Since these columns are crucial for spatial analysis, we will remove rows with missing values in these columns.
From Wikipedia, Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR) is the capital and most populous city of Thailand. It is located in the central part of the country, on the Chao Phraya River delta. The BMR consists of Bangkok and its surrounding provinces, including Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Samut Prakan, Nakhon Pathom, and Samut Sakhon. The dataset contains information on the location, severity, and date of accidents, which will be used for spatial and spatio-temporal point-pattern analysis.

bmr_acc_sf <- bmr_acc %>%
  filter(province_en == "Bangkok" | province_en == "Nonthaburi" | province_en == "Pathum Thani" | province_en == "Samut Prakan" | province_en == "Nakhon Pathom" | province_en == "Samut Sakhon") %>%
  #filter(year(incident_datetime) == 2022) %>%
  filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32647) # UTM Zone 47N (EPSG:32647) for Bangkok Metropolitan Region

Verifying that the missing values have been removed

null_counts_after <- sum(is.na(bmr_acc_sf))
null_counts_after

[1] 0
Next we check for duplicate records in the dataset. Duplicate records can skew the analysis and lead to inaccurate results. We will identify and remove any duplicate rows based on the acc_code column, which serves as a unique identifier for each accident.

# Check for duplicate records based on the 'acc_code' column
duplicates <- bmr_acc_sf[duplicated(bmr_acc_sf$acc_code), ]
nrow(duplicates)

[1] 0

For further analysis, we will focus on the road segments that are classified as “primary” roads, which are major roads that connect different regions and are likely to have higher traffic volumes. Identify road type for each accident event

bmr_roads <- read_rds("data/bmr_roads.rds")
bmr_acc_sf <- read_rds("data/bmr_road_traffic_accidents_2019-2022.rds")


# 1. index of the nearest road segment for every accident
nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(bmr_acc_sf, bmr_roads)


# 2. attach highway type + snapping distance
bmr_acc_sf <- bmr_acc_sf %>%
  mutate(
    highway = bmr_roads$highway[nearest_idx],
    dist_to_road_m = as.numeric(
      st_distance(bmr_acc_sf, bmr_roads[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)),
    # 3. only trust the match if the accident is close to the road
    highway = if_else(dist_to_road_m <= 50, highway, "off-network (>50 m)")
  )

This will make the spatial analysis more efficient and focused on the major roads that are likely to have higher traffic volumes and accident rates.



# save the filtered primary road network data for the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR) in RDS format for future use.
saveRDS(bmr_roads_filtered, file = "data/bmr_primary_roads.rds")

text:
5 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
In this section, we will perform exploratory data analysis (EDA) on the road traffic accident data for the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR). The goal of EDA is to understand the distribution and characteristics of the data, identify patterns and trends, and detect any anomalies or outliers that may affect the analysis.

5.1 Overall plot
Ploting 3 datasets onto a single choropleth map to have an general view.

tmap_mode('plot')

tm_shape(bmr_adm_boundary) +
  tm_polygons(col='adm1_name', alpha=0.6, border.col="black", lwd=0.7, title = "Region") +
  tm_shape(bmr_primary_roads) +
  tm_lines(col = "darkgreen", lwd=1, alpha = 0.8) +
  tm_shape(bmr_acc_sf) + 
  tm_dots(col = "red", size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) +                                     
  tm_layout(main.title = "Road Traffic Accidents in Bangkok Metropolitan Region (2019 - 2022) - primary road",
            main.title.position = "center",
            main.title.size = 3,
            #title.position = c("center", "top"),
            legend.position = c("left", "bottom"),
            legend.text.size = 0.6
            
  )














NoteNote



The overall plot provides a visual summary of the road traffic accidents in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR) for the year 2019 to 2022. It overlays the administrative boundaries, primary road network, and accident locations, allowing us to quickly identify areas with high accident density and their relation to major roads.
Observing the map, we can see that the majority of accidents are concentrated along the primary roads and in densely populated areas, highlighting the importance of focusing on these regions for traffic safety interventions.
This insight indicates that the 6 road types classified as primary roads are the most critical areas to target for traffic safety improvements and accident prevention measures.

acc_map

5.2 Visualization Geographic Distribution of Accidents by cause

# Calculate frequencies and plot
bmr_acc_sf %>%
  count(presumed_cause) %>%
  filter(n > 9) %>%
  # reorder() sorts the bars from highest to lowest frequency
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(presumed_cause, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +

Accidents by year and province

# calculate total accidents by year
bmr_acc_by_year <- bmr_acc_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(total_accidents = n())

# Calculate total accidents by province and year
bmr_acc_by_province_year <- bmr_acc_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(year, province_en) %>%
  summarise(total_accidents = n()) %>%
  ungroup()

# Summarise total accidents for each year (trend)
total_accidents_by_year <- bmr_acc_by_province_year %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(total_accidents = sum(total_accidents))

# create stacked bar chart for accidents by province and year
fig_acc_by_province_year <- ggplot(bmr_acc_by_province_year, aes(x = factor(year), y = total_accidents, fill = province_en)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Road Traffic Accidents by Province and Year",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Total Accidents",
       fill = "Province_en") +
  theme_minimal() +
  # add trend line for total accidents by year
  geom_line(data = total_accidents_by_year, 
  aes(x = factor(year), y = total_accidents, group = 1), 
  color = "black", size = 1,
  linetype = "dashed",
  inherit.aes = FALSE) 

fig_acc_by_province_year














Note




Accident trend is represented by the dashed black line in the stacked bar chart. The line indicate an uptrend in the total number of accidents over the years.
Bangkok consistently has the highest number of accidents compared to other provinces in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region.
The number of accidents of other provinces shows a relatively stable trend over the years.
The number of accidents in 2022 rises compared to previous years, it’s related to the rise in number of accidents in Bangkok and Samut Prakan.

fig_acc_by_month_province

The stacked bar chart shows the distribution of road traffic accidents by month and province.
The number of accidents spikes in certain months (e.g., April and December), indicating potential seasonal trends or periods of increased traffic activity.





5.5 Visualization Geographic Distribution of Accidents by day of the week

# mutate day of the week column
bmr_acc_sf <- bmr_acc_sf %>%
  mutate(day_of_week = lubridate::wday(incident_datetime, label = TRUE))

tm_shape(bmr_adm_boundary) +
  #tm_polygons(col='adm1_name', alpha=0.6, border.col="black", lwd=0.7, title = "Region") +

Bar chart accidents by days of the week

#compute accidents by day of the week 
accidents_by_day_of_week <- bmr_acc_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(
    day_type = case_when(
      day_of_week %in% c("Sat", "Sun") ~ "Weekend",
      TRUE ~ "Weekday"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(day_of_week, day_type) %>%
  summarise(total_accidents = n()) %>%
  ungroup()

Note




Weekdays generally have fewer accidents compared to weekends except for Friday.
Both Friday & Saturday have relatively high numbers of accidents suggesting increased traffic activity or risky driving behavior (possibly due to social events or nightlife - parties, gatherings, or late-night activities. Be noted that in general, people tend to drink more alcohol on Friday and Saturday nights).

title: Hands-on Exercise 03
text:
Spatio-temporal point process (space-time or spatial-temporal point process) is random collection of points, where each point represents the time and location of an event. Examples of events include incidence of disease, sightings or births of a species, or the occurrences of fires, earthquakes, lightning strikes, tsunamis, or volcanic eruptions.
This hands-on exercise used forest fires data to answer to answer the below questions: - are the locations of forest fire in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung spatial and spatio-temporally independent? - if the answer is NO, where and when the observed forest fire locations tend to cluster?






Notereference



r4gdsa chap 06 - Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis.





The 2 data sets in national level downloaded from Indonesia websites: - modis_2024_Indonesia.csv, MODIS data is downloaded from Fire Information for Resource Management System. - The Indonesia nationwide ESRI shapefile is downloaded from Indonesia Geospatial portal. Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung data later will be extracted from this data.




pacman::p_load(sf, spatstat, sparr, 
               tmap, stpp, tidyverse)




Importing the data into R environment.

sub_district <- st_read(dsn = "../../data/geospatial", 
                layer = "Batas_Wilayah_KelurahanDesa_10K_AR")

The original data has 83518 polygons, each polygons has 26 fields. It’s very heavy to keep reading this file so we need to extract the data for Bangka Belitung area only. After playing with the data, i found out that the province name is under WADMPR column.

grep("Bangka", sub_district$WADMPR, value = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE) |> unique()

Extracting Bangka Belitung area data:

kbb <- sub_district[sub_district$WADMPR == "Kepulauan Bangka Belitung", ]
nrow(kbb)

title: Hands-on Exercise 03
text:
Spatio-temporal point process (space-time or spatial-temporal point process) is random collection of points, where each point represents the time and location of an event. Examples of events include incidence of disease, sightings or births of a species, or the occurrences of fires, earthquakes, lightning strikes, tsunamis, or volcanic eruptions.
This hands-on exercise used forest fires data to answer to answer the below questions: - are the locations of forest fire in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung spatial and spatio-temporally independent? - if the answer is NO, where and when the observed forest fire locations tend to cluster?






Notereference



r4gdsa chap 06 - Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis.

R for Geospatial Data Science and Analytics - 2  Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R


In general, thematic mapping involves the use of map symbols to visualize selected properties of geographic features that are not naturally visible, such as population, temperature, crime rate, and property prices, just to mention a few of them.
Geovisualisation, on the other hand, is the process of using visual representations and cartographic techniques to explore, analyze, and communicate geospatial data. It combines elements of cartography, computer science, and information visualization to enhance spatial understanding and knowledge discovery.
In this chapter, you will learn how to plot functional and truthful choropleth maps by using an R package called tmap package.

Function to extract values from the HTML description:
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()

    fill = "DEPENDENCY")

  tm_polygons()














Note



By default, it plots areas of polygons in light gray (gray85) and polygons borders in slightly dark gray (gray25).





To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, we just need to assign the target variable such as Dependency to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")

  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()

The fill_alpha argument is used to define transparency number between 0 (totally transparent) and 1 (not transparent). By default, the alpha value of the col is used (normally 1).

col = border colour,
lwd = border line width. The default is 1, and
lty = border line type. The default is “solid”.

  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")

  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: Hands-on Exercise 01B
text:
In general, thematic mapping involves the use of map symbols to visualize selected properties of geographic features that are not naturally visible, such as population, temperature, crime rate, and property prices, just to mention a few of them.
Geovisualisation, on the other hand, is the process of using visual representations and cartographic techniques to explore, analyze, and communicate geospatial data. It combines elements of cartography, computer science, and information visualization to enhance spatial understanding and knowledge discovery.
In this chapter, you will learn how to plot functional and truthful choropleth maps by using an R package called tmap package.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {

title: Hands-on Exercise 01A
text:
R for Geospatial Data Science and Analytics - 1  Geospatial Data Science with R



installing and loading sf and tidyverse packages into R environment,
importing geospatial data by using appropriate functions of sf package,
importing aspatial data by using appropriate function of readr package,
exploring the content of simple feature data frame by using appropriate Base R and sf functions,
assigning or transforming coordinate systems by using using appropriate sf functions,
converting an aspatial data into a sf data frame by using appropriate function of sf package,
performing geoprocessing tasks by using appropriate functions of sf package,
performing data wrangling tasks by using appropriate functions of dplyr package and
performing Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) by using appropriate functions from ggplot2 package.







Dataset
Source
Description




Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web)
data.gov.sg
Geospatial boundaries for Singapore’s planning subzones.


Pre-Schools Location
data.gov.sg
Location data for pre-schools in Singapore.


Cycling Path
LTA DataMall
Geospatial data for cycling paths in Singapore.


Singapore Airbnb Listings
Inside Airbnb
Latest listing data for Airbnb properties in Singapore.






To get started, create a new folder called Hands-on_Ex in a working directory.
Next, create a new sub-folder called Hands-on_ex01 in the newly created Hands-on_Ex folder.
In the Hands-on_Ex01 folder, create a sub-folder called data. Then, inside the data sub-folder, create two sub-folders and name them geospatial and aspatial respectively.
Place Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web), Pre-Schools Location and Cycling Path zipped files into geospatial sub-folder and unzipped them. Copy the unzipped files from their respective sub-folders and place them inside geospatial sub-folder.
**1.2.2 Extracting the aspatial data set
** Now, you will extract the downloaded listing data file. At Downloads folder, cut and paste listing.csv into aspatial sub-folder.



In this hands-on exercise, two R packages will be used. They are:

sf for importing, managing, and processing geospatial data, and
tidyverse for performing data science tasks such as importing, wrangling and visualising data.

Tidyverse consists of a family of R packages. In this hands-on exercise, the following packages will be used:

readr for importing csv data,

tidyr for manipulating data,

dplyr for transforming data, and

ggplot2 for visualising data







Note



Tidyverse consists of a family of R packages. In this hands-on exercise, the following packages will be used:

readr for importing csv data,
tidyr for manipulating data,
dplyr for transforming data, and
ggplot2 for visualising data

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse)

The authority is planning to upgrade the exiting cycling path. To do so, they need to acquire 5 metres of reserved land on the both sides of the existing cycling path. You are tasked to determine the extend of the land need to be acquired and their total area.



Firstly, st_buffer() of sf package is used to compute the 5-meter buffers around cycling paths.

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(   cyclingpath, dist=5, nQuadSegs = 30)

This is followed by calculating the area of the buffers as shown in the code chunk below.

buffer_cycling$AREA <- st_area(buffer_cycling)

If you are tidyverse person like me, code chunk below should be used.

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%   mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))


sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

5317952 [m^2]


5317952 [m^2]
We can also create a plot showing the buffer by a selected planning subzone.
Assuming that we are interested on the land acquisition in Tampines West planning subzone.
Firstly, filter() of dplyr package will be used to extract polygon feature of Tampines West by using the code chunk below.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%   filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST") 







Note



You need to override the incorrect coordinate definition on mpsz_selected by explicitly setting it to WGS84 (EPSG 4326), and then transform it to the proper SVY21 metric system (EPSG 3414) to match your cycling data.


Run this block of code to fix the projection:

# 1. Force the correct WGS84 CRS definition onto the mislabeled subzone layer
mpsz_selected <- st_set_crs(mpsz_selected, 4326)

# 2. Transform the subzone layer coordinates to true SVY21 metres
mpsz_selected_svy21 <- st_transform(mpsz_selected, 3414)

# 3. Ensure your cycling layer is explicitly set to SVY21 as well
buffer_cycling <- st_transform(buffer_cycling, 3414)

# 4. Perform the intersection again
buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected_svy21)

# 5. Check the results
print(buffer_cycling_selected)

In this hands-on exercise, two R packages will be used. They are:

sf for importing, managing, and processing geospatial data, and
tidyverse for performing data science tasks such as importing, wrangling and visualising data.

Tidyverse consists of a family of R packages. In this hands-on exercise, the following packages will be used:

readr for importing csv data,

tidyr for manipulating data,

dplyr for transforming data, and

ggplot2 for visualising data

readr for importing csv data,

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 01A
text:
The authority is planning to upgrade the exiting cycling path. To do so, they need to acquire 5 metres of reserved land on the both sides of the existing cycling path. You are tasked to determine the extend of the land need to be acquired and their total area.



Firstly, st_buffer() of sf package is used to compute the 5-meter buffers around cycling paths.

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(   cyclingpath, dist=5, nQuadSegs = 30)

This is followed by calculating the area of the buffers as shown in the code chunk below.

buffer_cycling$AREA <- st_area(buffer_cycling)

If you are tidyverse person like me, code chunk below should be used.

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%   mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))


sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

5317952 [m^2]


5317952 [m^2]
We can also create a plot showing the buffer by a selected planning subzone.
Assuming that we are interested on the land acquisition in Tampines West planning subzone.
Firstly, filter() of dplyr package will be used to extract polygon feature of Tampines West by using the code chunk below.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%   filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST") 







Note



You need to override the incorrect coordinate definition on mpsz_selected by explicitly setting it to WGS84 (EPSG 4326), and then transform it to the proper SVY21 metric system (EPSG 3414) to match your cycling data.


Run this block of code to fix the projection:

# 1. Force the correct WGS84 CRS definition onto the mislabeled subzone layer
mpsz_selected <- st_set_crs(mpsz_selected, 4326)

# 2. Transform the subzone layer coordinates to true SVY21 metres
mpsz_selected_svy21 <- st_transform(mpsz_selected, 3414)

# 3. Ensure your cycling layer is explicitly set to SVY21 as well
buffer_cycling <- st_transform(buffer_cycling, 3414)

# 4. Perform the intersection again
buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected_svy21)

# 5. Check the results
print(buffer_cycling_selected)

title: Hands-on Exercise 02
text:
Spatial Point Pattern Analysis is the evaluation of the pattern, or distribution, of a set of points on a surface. It can refer to the actual spatial or temporal location of these points or also include data from point sources. It is one of the most fundamental concepts in geography and spatial analysis.
This exercise has 2 parts:
Part1 covers First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods which focus on understanding the intensity or density of points across a study area. It examines how the distribution of points varies over space, essentially identifying trends or patterns in point density. This type of analysis deals with the individual locations of points and their distribution, without considering interactions between them.
Part2 cover Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods which examine the spatial relationships between points in a pattern, specifically focusing on how the presence of one point influences the location of others. It goes beyond simply describing the overall density of points (first-order effects) by investigating clustering, dispersion, or randomness at various spatial scales.






Notereferences



r4gdsa chap 04 - First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
r4gdsa chap 05 - Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods





In this part, spatstat is used to perform commonly used 1st-PPA methods in order to answer the specific questions:

Are the children centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?
If the answer is not, then the next logical question is where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?

Clark-Even Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis Method & Kernel Density Estimation Method will be used to answer the above questions.


To provide answers to the questions above, two data sets will be used. They are:

Child Care Services data from data.gov.sg, a point feature data providing both location and attribute information of childcare centres.
Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea), a polygon feature data providing information of URA 2019 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundary data.

Perform the Clark-Evans test of aggregation for a spatial point pattern by using clarkevans.test() of spatstat.explore package.
The test hypotheses are:
Ho = The distribution of childcare services are randomly distributed.
H1= The distribution of childcare services are not randomly distributed.
The 95% confident interval will be used.
Perform the Clark-Evan test without CSR

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"))


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








ImportantQuiz answer:




Decision: Since the p-value (\(< 2.2 \times 10^{-16}\)) is well below the significance threshold of \(\alpha = 0.05\), we reject the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
Inference: With an aggregation index of \(R = 0.53532\) (\(R < 1\)), there is statistically significant evidence at the 95% confidence level to conclude that childcare centres in Singapore are spatially clustered rather than randomly distributed.









ImportantBusiness communication




Market Clustering & Co-location: Childcare facilities are heavily concentrated in specific geographical clusters rather than dispersed evenly across Singapore. This concentration typically aligns with densely populated residential estates (such as major HDB towns) and transit-accessible hubs where young families reside.
Competitive Density vs. Underserved Gaps: High-density zones indicate strong existing demand but also heightened commercial competition among operators. Conversely, areas with sparse coverage may reveal untapped market potential or underserved gaps requiring targeted facility planning or government support.



Perform the Clark-Evans test with CSR
Clark-Evans test with CSR using MonteCarlo method.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








ImportantStatistical conclusion & communication




Decision: Since the Monte Carlo p-value (\(p = 0.01\)) is less than the significance threshold \(\alpha = 0.05\), we reject the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
Inference: With an aggregation index of \(R = 0.53532\) (\(R < 1\)), there is statistically significant evidence at the 95% confidence level (based on 99 CSR simulations) that childcare centres in Singapore exhibit a spatially clustered pattern rather than random spatial dispersion.

Business communication:
Childcare centres are not uniformly scattered across Singapore; they naturally cluster around high-density demand nodes such as major residential towns (e.g., mature HDB estates) and key public transit interchanges where young working families live and commute.











NoteInfo



Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a valuable tool for visualising and analyzing first-order spatial point patterns. It is widely considered a method within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA) because it’s used to visualize and understand spatial data patterns by transforms discrete point data (like locations of childcare service, crime incidents or disease cases) into continuous density surfaces that reveal clusters and variations in event occurrences, without making prior assumptions about data distribution. It helps to begin understanding data distribution, identify hotspots, and explore relationships between spatial variables before performing more rigorous analysis.

Working with different automatic bandwidth methods






Tipautomatic bandwidth methods in spatstat











Function
Method / Description
Best Used For


bw.diggle()
Cross-validation (Diggle’s method): Minimizes the mean squared error (MSE) between the estimated and true intensity.
Detecting a single tight cluster amidst random noise.


bw.ppl()
Likelihood Cross-Validation: Selects bandwidth by maximizing the leave-one-out cross-validated log-likelihood.
Patterns predominantly composed of tight clusters.


bw.CvL()
Cronie and van Lieshout’s method: Based on the Campbell formula to select bandwidth.
Point patterns where points are closely packed or general spatial trends.


bw.scott()
Scott’s Rule of Thumb: Computes separate bandwidths for the x and y dimensions based on standard deviations and sample size.
Fast parametric approximation across anisotropic (directional) spatial patterns.

Working with different kernel methods






TipKernel methods used in density.ppp()



In spatstat, the kernel smoothing function (passed via the kernel argument in density.ppp()) defines the weighting shape used to spread each point’s mass across the surface.
Available Kernel Methods

"gaussian" (Default): A bell-shaped normal distribution curve. It produces the smoothest surface and extends infinitely (truncated computationally), making it the standard choice for most point pattern analyses.
"epanechnikov": A inverted parabolic kernel (\(1 - r^2\)). It is mathematically optimal in minimizing asymptotic mean integrated squared error (MISE) and has bounded, finite support.
"quartic" (or Biweight): A smooth, bell-like polynomial function with finite support (\((1 - r^2)^2\)). It drops off more steeply at the boundaries than Gaussian while remaining smoother than Epanechnikov.
"disc": A flat, uniform cylindrical kernel where all points within the bandwidth radius receive equal weight, resulting in sharp, step-like density transitions.

             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE,

plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712,

Computing KDE by using adaptive bandwidth
Derive adaptive kernel density estimation by using density.adaptive() of spatstat.

  childcareSG_ppp_km, 
  method="kernel")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab)








Compare the fixed and adaptive kernel density estimation outputs

plot(kde_childcareSG_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")














Note











Feature
Fixed Bandwidth KDE
Adaptive Bandwidth KDE


Bandwidth Radius (\(\sigma\))
Constant across the entire study region. Every point uses the exact same search radius (e.g., 600 m).
Variable across space. The radius adjusts dynamically based on local point density.


High-Density Areas (e.g., Urban hubs)
May oversmooth distinct local clusters and merge separate peaks together.
Narrows the bandwidth (smaller \(\sigma\)) to capture sharper, local hotspot peaks.


Low-Density Areas (e.g., Rural / Periphery)
Leaves excessive empty space or creates artificial, isolated noise spikes around solitary points.
Widens the bandwidth (larger \(\sigma\)) to smooth out noise and provide meaningful generalized trends.


Best Used For

Second-order spatial point pattern analysis examines the spatial relationships between points in a pattern, specifically focusing on how the presence of one point influences the location of others. It goes beyond simply describing the overall density of points (first-order effects) by investigating clustering, dispersion, or randomness at various spatial scales.
In this part, appropriate functions of spatstat are used to discover the spatial point processes of childcare centres in Singapore to answer the specific questions:

are the children centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?
if the answer is not, then the next logical question is where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?







Noterefereces



Methods used for second-order spatial point pattern analysis








Method / Function
Purpose
Interpretation relative to CSR


G-Function


Gest()
Measures the cumulative distribution of distances from an arbitrary event to its nearest event.
• Above CSR: Clustering


• Below CSR: Regularity / Dispersion


F-Function


Fest()
Measures the distribution of distances from an arbitrary point in space to the nearest observed event (empty space function).
• Below CSR: Clustering (larger empty spaces)


• Above CSR: Regularity / Dispersion


K-Function


Kest()
Evaluates the expected number of events within distance \(r\) of a typical event, normalized by intensity.
• Above CSR: Clustering at scale \(r\)


• Below CSR: Regularity / Dispersion


L-Function


Lest()
Linearized, variance-stabilized transformation of Ripley’s K-function, typically plotted as \(L(r) - r\).
• \(L(r) - r > 0\): Clustering


• \(L(r) - r < 0\): Regularity / Dispersion


• \(L(r) - r = 0\): Complete Spatial Randomness


Monte Carlo Envelopes


envelope()
Generates simulation envelopes (critical bands) under CSR to statistically test null hypotheses (\(H_0\)).
• Outside Envelope: Significant departure from CSR (\(p < \alpha\))


• Inside Envelope: Cannot reject CSR

The Clark-Evans test is a distance-based statistical method used in Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) to determine whether a spatial point pattern exhibits clustering, regularity (dispersion), or Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).
Key Concept & Aggregation Index (\(R\))
The test compares the mean observed nearest neighbor distance (\(\bar{r}_O\)) to the expected mean distance under CSR (\(\bar{r}_E\)):
$$R = \frac{\bar{r}_O}{\bar{r}_E}$$

\(R = 1\): The pattern is randomly distributed (consistent with CSR).
\(R < 1\): Observed points are closer together than expected \(\rightarrow\) Clustered pattern.
\(R > 1\): Observed points are farther apart than expected \(\rightarrow\) Regular / Dispersed pattern (\(R \approx 2.15\) indicates a perfectly hexagonal lattice).

Hypothesis Testing

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The point events are randomly distributed across the study region.
Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): The point events are not randomly distributed (or specifically clustered: \(R < 1\), or regular: \(R > 1\)).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
In R, the test is performed using clarkevans.test() from the spatstat.explore package.

Standard Z-Test:
R
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,                  correction = "none",                  
clipregion = "sg_owin",                  
alternative = "clustered") 
Monte Carlo Simulation Test:
Compares the observed \(R\) value against simulated realizations of CSR to derive an exact empirical \(p\)-value:
R
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,                     correction = "none",                  
clipregion = "sg_owin",                  
alternative = "clustered",                  
method = "MonteCarlo",                  
nsim = 999) 




Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a fundamental first-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis (1st-SPPA) technique used within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA). It transforms discrete, observed point events into a continuous density surface, revealing spatial hotspots and variations in event intensity without imposing strict parametric assumptions.
Core Mechanics in spatstat

Basic Function: Computed using density() on a planar point pattern (ppp) object.
Pixel Image Output: The resulting object belongs to class im, representing a 2D regular pixel array where each cell contains the estimated point density.
Unit Rescaling: Because default projected coordinates (such as SVY21 in meters) produce very small numbers (points per \(\text{m}^2\)), rescale.ppp() is commonly applied to convert units to kilometers (points per \(\text{km}^2\)) for clearer interpretation.

Key Tuning Parameters & Methods

Bandwidth (\(\sigma\)) Selection: Controls the degree of smoothing.



bw.diggle(): Optimal for detecting isolated, tight clusters amidst random noise.
bw.ppl(): Recommended when the point pattern predominantly consists of tight clusters.
bw.CvL() & bw.scott(): Alternative cross-validation and rule-of-thumb bandwidth estimators.

Kernel Smoothing Types: Defines the weighting function around each point (gaussian by default, epanechnikov, quartic, or disc).
Edge Correction: Setting edge = TRUE adjusts for intensity underestimation near the study boundary (window border).
Fixed vs. Adaptive Bandwidth:



Fixed (density()): Uses a uniform bandwidth \(\sigma\) across the entire region; sensitive to areas with extreme density variations (e.g., dense urban centers vs. sparse rural areas).
Adaptive (adaptive.density()): Dynamically adjusts the bandwidth based on local point concentration, applying smaller kernels in dense areas and wider kernels in sparse zones.


Cartographic Visualization Pipeline
To generate presentation-ready maps using packages like tmap:

Convert the spatstat im object to a raster using rast() from the terra package.
Assign the coordinate reference system (e.g., crs(kde_raster) <- "EPSG:3414").
Render continuous choropleth surfaces using tm_shape() + tm_raster().




K-Function is a multi-scale second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that evaluates the spatial dependence (clustering, dispersion, or randomness) between point events across varying distance scales (\(r\)).
Unlike nearest-neighbor statistics (e.g., Clark-Evans or the G-function) which focus solely on the single closest point, the K-function evaluates the total number of points within a radius \(r\) around every typical point.
Mathematical Concept
The theoretical K-function is defined as:
$$K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda} E[\text{number of extra points within distance } r \text{ of an arbitrary point}]$$

\(\lambda\) represents the mean point intensity across the study region.
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), the expected number of points within radius \(r\) is \(\lambda \pi r^2\), giving the theoretical baseline:


$$K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2$$

Interpretation of Results

\(K(r) > \pi r^2\): More points are observed within radius \(r\) than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) < \pi r^2\): Fewer points are observed within radius \(r\) than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) = \pi r^2\): Pattern aligns with Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using the Kest() and envelope() functions from spatstat:

Computing the Empirical K-Function:


R
# Estimate K with edge correction (e.g., Ripley/isotropic)
K_est <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot K(r) centered against r (K(r) - r vs r) 
plot(K_est, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Testing Complete Spatial Randomness (Monte Carlo Simulation):


R
# Generate Monte Carlo simulation envelopes 
K_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed K against simulation envelopes 
plot(K_csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r") 

If the observed curve lies above the upper envelope, clustering is statistically significant (\(p < \alpha\)).
If the curve lies below the lower envelope, dispersion/regularity is statistically significant.





The G-Function (Nearest Neighbor Distance Distribution Function) is a second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that measures the cumulative distribution of distances from an arbitrary event to its nearest neighboring event.
Key Mathematical Concept
The function estimates the probability \(G(r)\) that an event’s nearest neighbor is located within a radial distance \(r\):
$$G(r) = P(d_i \le r)$$
Under the null hypothesis of Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), the theoretical distribution \(G_{theo}(r)\) for a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda\) is:
$$G_{theo}(r) = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)$$
Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(G(r) > G_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises faster than expected at short distances, indicating that events are located closer to one another \(\rightarrow\) Clustering.
\(G(r) < G_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises slower than expected, indicating events maintain distance from one another \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion.
\(G(r) \approx G_{theo}(r)\): The point pattern conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)

Estimation with Edge Correction:
Edge corrections (such as "border", "hanisch", or "best") adjust for unobserved points beyond the study boundary:


R
# Compute G-function estimation 
G_est <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical G(r) 
plot(G_est, xlim = c(0, 500)) 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:
Uses envelope() to generate Monte Carlo simulation critical bands:


R
# Monte Carlo simulation test under CSR (e.g., 999 simulations) 
G_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, correction = "all", nsim = 999)  

# Plot observed G(r) against simulation envelope 
plot(G_csr) 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).





The F-Function (also known as the Empty Space Function or point-to-event distance distribution) is a second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that measures the distribution of distances from an arbitrary location in the study area to the nearest observed event.
Unlike the G-function (which measures distances between event pairs), the F-function samples the empty space across the entire study window.
Mathematical Concept
The function estimates the cumulative probability \(F(r)\) that an arbitrary point chosen at random within the observation window has at least one event within radial distance \(r\):
$$F(r) = P(d(x, Y) \le r)$$
where \(d(x, Y)\) is the shortest distance from an arbitrary point \(x\) to the nearest event in point pattern \(Y\).
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) for a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda\), the theoretical baseline is:
$$F_{theo}(r) = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)$$
Interpretation Relative to CSR
Because the F-function measures empty spaces:

\(F(r) < F_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises slower than CSR, meaning empty spaces are larger than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Clustering (events group together, leaving wide gaps).
\(F(r) > F_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises faster than CSR, meaning points are evenly spread throughout the space \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion.
\(F(r) \approx F_{theo}(r)\): The pattern conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using the Fest() and envelope() functions from spatstat:

Computing the Empirical F-Function:


R
# Estimate F with edge correction (e.g., "best" or "raw") 
F_ck <- Fest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "best")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical F(r) 
plot(F_ck) 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:


R
# Monte Carlo simulation test under CSR (e.g., 999 simulations) 
F_ck_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Fest, nsim = 999)  

# Plot observed F(r) against simulation envelopes 
plot(F_ck_csr) 

Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant clustering (\(p < \alpha\)).
Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion (\(p < \alpha\)).





The K-Function (Ripley’s K-Function) is a multi-scale second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method used to evaluate whether point events exhibit clustering, dispersion, or randomness across multiple distance scales (\(r\)).
Unlike nearest-neighbor statistics, which only consider the distance to the single closest point, the K-function evaluates the total number of points found within a given radius \(r\) of any arbitrary point.
Mathematical Concept
The theoretical K-function is defined as:
$$K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda} \mathbb{E}[\text{number of additional events within distance } r \text{ of a typical event}]$$

\(\lambda\) is the overall intensity of the point pattern.
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) for a homogeneous Poisson process, the expected number of events within radius \(r\) is \(\lambda \pi r^2\), yielding the theoretical baseline:


$$K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2$$

Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(K(r) > \pi r^2\): More events are observed within distance \(r\) than expected under randomness \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) < \pi r^2\): Fewer events are observed within distance \(r\) than expected \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) = \pi r^2\): Follows Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)

Computing Empirical K-Function:
Estimated using Kest() with an edge-correction method (such as Ripley’s isotropic correction):


R
# Estimate K-function 
K_ck <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical K(r) centered against r (K(r) - r vs r) 
plot(K_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:
Evaluated using envelope() to run Monte Carlo simulations and establish critical confidence bands:


R
# Run Monte Carlo simulation envelopes under CSR 
K_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed K against simulation envelopes 
plot(K_ck.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r") 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).





The L-Function (Besag’s L-Function) is a variance-stabilized, linearized transformation of Ripley’s K-Function used in second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis.
While the K-function grows quadratically with distance (\(K(r) \approx \pi r^2\) under Complete Spatial Randomness), the L-function transforms this into a linear relationship, making departures from randomness easier to visually inspect and interpret across distance scales (\(r\)).
Mathematical Concept
Besag’s transformation scales the K-function as:
$$L(r) = \sqrt{\frac{K(r)}{\pi}}$$
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), \(K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2\), which simplifies to:
$$L_{theo}(r) = r \quad \iff \quad L(r) - r = 0$$
In practice, the L-function is almost always analyzed and plotted as the centered function \(L(r) - r\) (or \(L(d) - d\)) against distance \(r\).
Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(L(r) - r > 0\): Observed spatial density within radius \(r\) exceeds CSR expectation \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(L(r) - r < 0\): Observed spatial density within radius \(r\) is less than CSR expectation \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(L(r) - r = 0\): Conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using Lest() and envelope() from spatstat:

Computing Empirical L-Function:


R
# Estimate L-function with edge correction (e.g., Ripley/isotropic) 
L_ck <- Lest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot centered L(r) - r against distance r 
plot(L_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:


R
# Generate Monte Carlo simulation envelopes under CSR 
L_ck_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed L(r) - r against the simulation envelope 
plot(L_ck_csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "L(d)-r") 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at distance \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at distance \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Inside Envelopes: No statistically significant departure from CSR.

title: Hands-on Exercise 02
text:
Spatial Point Pattern Analysis is the evaluation of the pattern, or distribution, of a set of points on a surface. It can refer to the actual spatial or temporal location of these points or also include data from point sources. It is one of the most fundamental concepts in geography and spatial analysis.
This exercise has 2 parts:
Part1 covers First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods which focus on understanding the intensity or density of points across a study area. It examines how the distribution of points varies over space, essentially identifying trends or patterns in point density. This type of analysis deals with the individual locations of points and their distribution, without considering interactions between them.
Part2 cover Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods which examine the spatial relationships between points in a pattern, specifically focusing on how the presence of one point influences the location of others. It goes beyond simply describing the overall density of points (first-order effects) by investigating clustering, dispersion, or randomness at various spatial scales.






Notereferences



r4gdsa chap 04 - First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
r4gdsa chap 05 - Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods

In this part, spatstat is used to perform commonly used 1st-PPA methods in order to answer the specific questions:

Are the children centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?
If the answer is not, then the next logical question is where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?

Clark-Even Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis Method & Kernel Density Estimation Method will be used to answer the above questions.

Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) is a spatial statistics method that calculates the average distance between each point and its closest neighbor to determine if a pattern of points is clustered, dispersed, or randomly distributed.


Perform the Clark-Evans test of aggregation for a spatial point pattern by using clarkevans.test() of spatstat.explore package.
The test hypotheses are:
Ho = The distribution of childcare services are randomly distributed.
H1= The distribution of childcare services are not randomly distributed.
The 95% confident interval will be used.
Perform the Clark-Evan test without CSR

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"))


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








ImportantQuiz answer:




Decision: Since the p-value (\(< 2.2 \times 10^{-16}\)) is well below the significance threshold of \(\alpha = 0.05\), we reject the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
Inference: With an aggregation index of \(R = 0.53532\) (\(R < 1\)), there is statistically significant evidence at the 95% confidence level to conclude that childcare centres in Singapore are spatially clustered rather than randomly distributed.









ImportantBusiness communication




Market Clustering & Co-location: Childcare facilities are heavily concentrated in specific geographical clusters rather than dispersed evenly across Singapore. This concentration typically aligns with densely populated residential estates (such as major HDB towns) and transit-accessible hubs where young families reside.
Competitive Density vs. Underserved Gaps: High-density zones indicate strong existing demand but also heightened commercial competition among operators. Conversely, areas with sparse coverage may reveal untapped market potential or underserved gaps requiring targeted facility planning or government support.



Perform the Clark-Evans test with CSR
Clark-Evans test with CSR using MonteCarlo method.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








ImportantStatistical conclusion & communication




Decision: Since the Monte Carlo p-value (\(p = 0.01\)) is less than the significance threshold \(\alpha = 0.05\), we reject the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
Inference: With an aggregation index of \(R = 0.53532\) (\(R < 1\)), there is statistically significant evidence at the 95% confidence level (based on 99 CSR simulations) that childcare centres in Singapore exhibit a spatially clustered pattern rather than random spatial dispersion.

Business communication:
Childcare centres are not uniformly scattered across Singapore; they naturally cluster around high-density demand nodes such as major residential towns (e.g., mature HDB estates) and key public transit interchanges where young working families live and commute.











NoteInfo



Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a valuable tool for visualising and analyzing first-order spatial point patterns. It is widely considered a method within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA) because it’s used to visualize and understand spatial data patterns by transforms discrete point data (like locations of childcare service, crime incidents or disease cases) into continuous density surfaces that reveal clusters and variations in event occurrences, without making prior assumptions about data distribution. It helps to begin understanding data distribution, identify hotspots, and explore relationships between spatial variables before performing more rigorous analysis.

Compute a kernel density by using density() of spatstat:

kde_SG_diggle <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  sigma=bw.diggle,
  edge=TRUE,

Working with different automatic bandwidth methods






Tipautomatic bandwidth methods in spatstat











Function
Method / Description
Best Used For


bw.diggle()
Cross-validation (Diggle’s method): Minimizes the mean squared error (MSE) between the estimated and true intensity.
Detecting a single tight cluster amidst random noise.


bw.ppl()
Likelihood Cross-Validation: Selects bandwidth by maximizing the leave-one-out cross-validated log-likelihood.
Patterns predominantly composed of tight clusters.


bw.CvL()
Cronie and van Lieshout’s method: Based on the Campbell formula to select bandwidth.
Point patterns where points are closely packed or general spatial trends.


bw.scott()
Scott’s Rule of Thumb: Computes separate bandwidths for the x and y dimensions based on standard deviations and sample size.
Fast parametric approximation across anisotropic (directional) spatial patterns.

plot(kde_childcareSG.ppl, main = "bw.ppl")








Working with different kernel methods






TipKernel methods used in density.ppp()



In spatstat, the kernel smoothing function (passed via the kernel argument in density.ppp()) defines the weighting shape used to spread each point’s mass across the surface.
Available Kernel Methods

"gaussian" (Default): A bell-shaped normal distribution curve. It produces the smoothest surface and extends infinitely (truncated computationally), making it the standard choice for most point pattern analyses.
"epanechnikov": A inverted parabolic kernel (\(1 - r^2\)). It is mathematically optimal in minimizing asymptotic mean integrated squared error (MISE) and has bounded, finite support.
"quartic" (or Biweight): A smooth, bell-like polynomial function with finite support (\((1 - r^2)^2\)). It drops off more steeply at the boundaries than Gaussian while remaining smoother than Epanechnikov.
"disc": A flat, uniform cylindrical kernel where all points within the bandwidth radius receive equal weight, resulting in sharp, step-like density transitions.




par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"), 
     main="Gaussian")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="epanechnikov"), 
     main="Epanechnikov")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="quartic"), 
     main="Quartic")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="disc"), 
     main="Disc")

Computing KDE by using fixed bandwidth
In this sample, we will compute a KDE layer by defining a bandwidth of 600 meter.

kde_childcareSG_fb <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                              sigma=0.6,

                              kernel="gaussian")
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb)








Computing KDE by using adaptive bandwidth
Derive adaptive kernel density estimation by using density.adaptive() of spatstat.

kde_childcareSG_ab <- adaptive.density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km, 
  method="kernel")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab)








Compare the fixed and adaptive kernel density estimation outputs

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")














Note











Feature
Fixed Bandwidth KDE
Adaptive Bandwidth KDE


Bandwidth Radius (\(\sigma\))
Constant across the entire study region. Every point uses the exact same search radius (e.g., 600 m).
Variable across space. The radius adjusts dynamically based on local point density.


High-Density Areas (e.g., Urban hubs)
May oversmooth distinct local clusters and merge separate peaks together.
Narrows the bandwidth (smaller \(\sigma\)) to capture sharper, local hotspot peaks.


Low-Density Areas (e.g., Rural / Periphery)
Leaves excessive empty space or creates artificial, isolated noise spikes around solitary points.
Widens the bandwidth (larger \(\sigma\)) to smooth out noise and provide meaningful generalized trends.


Best Used For
Homogeneous point distributions or when comparing absolute density across regions with standard units.
Highly skewed distributions where point densities vary drastically across urban and rural/peripheral landscapes.


Implementation in spatstat
density(childcare_ppp, sigma = 0.6)
adaptive.density(childcare_ppp, method = "kernel")

title: Hands-on Exercise 02
text:
The Clark-Evans test is a distance-based statistical method used in Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) to determine whether a spatial point pattern exhibits clustering, regularity (dispersion), or Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).
Key Concept & Aggregation Index (\(R\))
The test compares the mean observed nearest neighbor distance (\(\bar{r}_O\)) to the expected mean distance under CSR (\(\bar{r}_E\)):
$$R = \frac{\bar{r}_O}{\bar{r}_E}$$

\(R = 1\): The pattern is randomly distributed (consistent with CSR).
\(R < 1\): Observed points are closer together than expected \(\rightarrow\) Clustered pattern.
\(R > 1\): Observed points are farther apart than expected \(\rightarrow\) Regular / Dispersed pattern (\(R \approx 2.15\) indicates a perfectly hexagonal lattice).

Hypothesis Testing

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The point events are randomly distributed across the study region.
Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): The point events are not randomly distributed (or specifically clustered: \(R < 1\), or regular: \(R > 1\)).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
In R, the test is performed using clarkevans.test() from the spatstat.explore package.

Standard Z-Test:
R
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,                  correction = "none",                  
clipregion = "sg_owin",                  
alternative = "clustered") 
Monte Carlo Simulation Test:
Compares the observed \(R\) value against simulated realizations of CSR to derive an exact empirical \(p\)-value:
R
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,                     correction = "none",                  
clipregion = "sg_owin",                  
alternative = "clustered",                  
method = "MonteCarlo",                  
nsim = 999) 




Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a fundamental first-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis (1st-SPPA) technique used within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA). It transforms discrete, observed point events into a continuous density surface, revealing spatial hotspots and variations in event intensity without imposing strict parametric assumptions.
Core Mechanics in spatstat

Basic Function: Computed using density() on a planar point pattern (ppp) object.
Pixel Image Output: The resulting object belongs to class im, representing a 2D regular pixel array where each cell contains the estimated point density.
Unit Rescaling: Because default projected coordinates (such as SVY21 in meters) produce very small numbers (points per \(\text{m}^2\)), rescale.ppp() is commonly applied to convert units to kilometers (points per \(\text{km}^2\)) for clearer interpretation.

Key Tuning Parameters & Methods

Bandwidth (\(\sigma\)) Selection: Controls the degree of smoothing.



bw.diggle(): Optimal for detecting isolated, tight clusters amidst random noise.
bw.ppl(): Recommended when the point pattern predominantly consists of tight clusters.
bw.CvL() & bw.scott(): Alternative cross-validation and rule-of-thumb bandwidth estimators.

Kernel Smoothing Types: Defines the weighting function around each point (gaussian by default, epanechnikov, quartic, or disc).
Edge Correction: Setting edge = TRUE adjusts for intensity underestimation near the study boundary (window border).
Fixed vs. Adaptive Bandwidth:



Fixed (density()): Uses a uniform bandwidth \(\sigma\) across the entire region; sensitive to areas with extreme density variations (e.g., dense urban centers vs. sparse rural areas).
Adaptive (adaptive.density()): Dynamically adjusts the bandwidth based on local point concentration, applying smaller kernels in dense areas and wider kernels in sparse zones.


Cartographic Visualization Pipeline
To generate presentation-ready maps using packages like tmap:

Convert the spatstat im object to a raster using rast() from the terra package.
Assign the coordinate reference system (e.g., crs(kde_raster) <- "EPSG:3414").
Render continuous choropleth surfaces using tm_shape() + tm_raster().




K-Function is a multi-scale second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that evaluates the spatial dependence (clustering, dispersion, or randomness) between point events across varying distance scales (\(r\)).
Unlike nearest-neighbor statistics (e.g., Clark-Evans or the G-function) which focus solely on the single closest point, the K-function evaluates the total number of points within a radius \(r\) around every typical point.
Mathematical Concept
The theoretical K-function is defined as:
$$K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda} E[\text{number of extra points within distance } r \text{ of an arbitrary point}]$$

\(\lambda\) represents the mean point intensity across the study region.
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), the expected number of points within radius \(r\) is \(\lambda \pi r^2\), giving the theoretical baseline:


$$K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2$$

Interpretation of Results

\(K(r) > \pi r^2\): More points are observed within radius \(r\) than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) < \pi r^2\): Fewer points are observed within radius \(r\) than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) = \pi r^2\): Pattern aligns with Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using the Kest() and envelope() functions from spatstat:

Computing the Empirical K-Function:


R
# Estimate K with edge correction (e.g., Ripley/isotropic)
K_est <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot K(r) centered against r (K(r) - r vs r) 
plot(K_est, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Testing Complete Spatial Randomness (Monte Carlo Simulation):


R
# Generate Monte Carlo simulation envelopes 
K_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed K against simulation envelopes 
plot(K_csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r") 

If the observed curve lies above the upper envelope, clustering is statistically significant (\(p < \alpha\)).
If the curve lies below the lower envelope, dispersion/regularity is statistically significant.





The G-Function (Nearest Neighbor Distance Distribution Function) is a second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that measures the cumulative distribution of distances from an arbitrary event to its nearest neighboring event.
Key Mathematical Concept
The function estimates the probability \(G(r)\) that an event’s nearest neighbor is located within a radial distance \(r\):
$$G(r) = P(d_i \le r)$$
Under the null hypothesis of Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), the theoretical distribution \(G_{theo}(r)\) for a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda\) is:
$$G_{theo}(r) = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)$$
Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(G(r) > G_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises faster than expected at short distances, indicating that events are located closer to one another \(\rightarrow\) Clustering.
\(G(r) < G_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises slower than expected, indicating events maintain distance from one another \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion.
\(G(r) \approx G_{theo}(r)\): The point pattern conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)

Estimation with Edge Correction:
Edge corrections (such as "border", "hanisch", or "best") adjust for unobserved points beyond the study boundary:


R
# Compute G-function estimation 
G_est <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical G(r) 
plot(G_est, xlim = c(0, 500)) 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:
Uses envelope() to generate Monte Carlo simulation critical bands:


R
# Monte Carlo simulation test under CSR (e.g., 999 simulations) 
G_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Gest, correction = "all", nsim = 999)  

# Plot observed G(r) against simulation envelope 
plot(G_csr) 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).





The F-Function (also known as the Empty Space Function or point-to-event distance distribution) is a second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method that measures the distribution of distances from an arbitrary location in the study area to the nearest observed event.
Unlike the G-function (which measures distances between event pairs), the F-function samples the empty space across the entire study window.
Mathematical Concept
The function estimates the cumulative probability \(F(r)\) that an arbitrary point chosen at random within the observation window has at least one event within radial distance \(r\):
$$F(r) = P(d(x, Y) \le r)$$
where \(d(x, Y)\) is the shortest distance from an arbitrary point \(x\) to the nearest event in point pattern \(Y\).
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) for a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda\), the theoretical baseline is:
$$F_{theo}(r) = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)$$
Interpretation Relative to CSR
Because the F-function measures empty spaces:

\(F(r) < F_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises slower than CSR, meaning empty spaces are larger than expected by chance \(\rightarrow\) Clustering (events group together, leaving wide gaps).
\(F(r) > F_{theo}(r)\): The curve rises faster than CSR, meaning points are evenly spread throughout the space \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion.
\(F(r) \approx F_{theo}(r)\): The pattern conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using the Fest() and envelope() functions from spatstat:

Computing the Empirical F-Function:


R
# Estimate F with edge correction (e.g., "best" or "raw") 
F_ck <- Fest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "best")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical F(r) 
plot(F_ck) 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:


R
# Monte Carlo simulation test under CSR (e.g., 999 simulations) 
F_ck_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Fest, nsim = 999)  

# Plot observed F(r) against simulation envelopes 
plot(F_ck_csr) 

Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant clustering (\(p < \alpha\)).
Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion (\(p < \alpha\)).





The K-Function (Ripley’s K-Function) is a multi-scale second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis method used to evaluate whether point events exhibit clustering, dispersion, or randomness across multiple distance scales (\(r\)).
Unlike nearest-neighbor statistics, which only consider the distance to the single closest point, the K-function evaluates the total number of points found within a given radius \(r\) of any arbitrary point.
Mathematical Concept
The theoretical K-function is defined as:
$$K(r) = \frac{1}{\lambda} \mathbb{E}[\text{number of additional events within distance } r \text{ of a typical event}]$$

\(\lambda\) is the overall intensity of the point pattern.
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) for a homogeneous Poisson process, the expected number of events within radius \(r\) is \(\lambda \pi r^2\), yielding the theoretical baseline:


$$K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2$$

Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(K(r) > \pi r^2\): More events are observed within distance \(r\) than expected under randomness \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) < \pi r^2\): Fewer events are observed within distance \(r\) than expected \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(K(r) = \pi r^2\): Follows Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)

Computing Empirical K-Function:
Estimated using Kest() with an edge-correction method (such as Ripley’s isotropic correction):


R
# Estimate K-function 
K_ck <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot empirical vs theoretical K(r) centered against r (K(r) - r vs r) 
plot(K_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:
Evaluated using envelope() to run Monte Carlo simulations and establish critical confidence bands:


R
# Run Monte Carlo simulation envelopes under CSR 
K_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed K against simulation envelopes 
plot(K_ck.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r") 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at scale \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).





The L-Function (Besag’s L-Function) is a variance-stabilized, linearized transformation of Ripley’s K-Function used in second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis.
While the K-function grows quadratically with distance (\(K(r) \approx \pi r^2\) under Complete Spatial Randomness), the L-function transforms this into a linear relationship, making departures from randomness easier to visually inspect and interpret across distance scales (\(r\)).
Mathematical Concept
Besag’s transformation scales the K-function as:
$$L(r) = \sqrt{\frac{K(r)}{\pi}}$$
Under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR), \(K_{theo}(r) = \pi r^2\), which simplifies to:
$$L_{theo}(r) = r \quad \iff \quad L(r) - r = 0$$
In practice, the L-function is almost always analyzed and plotted as the centered function \(L(r) - r\) (or \(L(d) - d\)) against distance \(r\).
Interpretation Relative to CSR

\(L(r) - r > 0\): Observed spatial density within radius \(r\) exceeds CSR expectation \(\rightarrow\) Clustering at scale \(r\).
\(L(r) - r < 0\): Observed spatial density within radius \(r\) is less than CSR expectation \(\rightarrow\) Regularity / Dispersion at scale \(r\).
\(L(r) - r = 0\): Conforms to Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR).

Implementation in R (spatstat)
Using Lest() and envelope() from spatstat:

Computing Empirical L-Function:


R
# Estimate L-function with edge correction (e.g., Ripley/isotropic) 
L_ck <- Lest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")  

# Plot centered L(r) - r against distance r 
plot(L_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)") 
Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) Hypothesis Testing:


R
# Generate Monte Carlo simulation envelopes under CSR 
L_ck_csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)  

# Plot observed L(r) - r against the simulation envelope 
plot(L_ck_csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "L(d)-r") 

Above Upper Envelope: Statistically significant clustering at distance \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Below Lower Envelope: Statistically significant regularity/dispersion at distance \(r\) (\(p < \alpha\)).
Inside Envelopes: No statistically significant departure from CSR.

In this section, we will use dnearneigh() of spdap package to derive distance-based weight matrices.
The function identifies neighbours of region points by Euclidean distance with a distance band with lower d1= and upper d2= bounds controlled by the bounds= argument. If unprojected coordinates are used and either specified in the coordinates object x or with x as a two column matrix and longlat=TRUE, great circle distances in km will be calculated assuming the WGS84 reference ellipsoid.


To determine the upper limit of distance band by using below steps:

Return a matrix with the indices of points belonging to the set of the k nearest neighbours of each other by using knearneigh() of spdep.
Convert the knn object returned by knearneigh() into a neighbours list of class nb with a list of integer vectors containing neighbour region number ids by using knn2nb().
Return the length of neighbour relationship edges by using nbdists() of spdep. The function returns in the units of the coordinates if the coordinates are projected, in km otherwise.
Remove the list structure of the returned object by using unlist().


#coords <- coordinates(hunan)
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

TipQuiz answer



Q: What is the meaning of “Average number of links: 3.681818”?
A:
The “Average number of links: 3.681818” means that, on average across your spatial dataset, each region has approximately 3.68 neighbors.
Here is how that number is calculated and what it represents:

The Calculation:
$$\text{Average Links} = \frac{\text{Total Nonzero Links}}{\text{Total Regions}} = \frac{324}{88} \approx 3.681818$$

One of the characteristics of fixed distance weight matrix is that more densely settled areas (usually the urban areas) tend to have more neighbours and the less densely settled areas (usually the rural counties) tend to have lesser neighbours. Having many neighbours smoothes the neighbour relationship across more neighbours.

In this section, we need to assign weights to each neighboring polygon. In our case, each neighboring polygon will be assigned equal weight (style=“W”). This is accomplished by assigning the fraction 1/(#ofneighbors) to each neighboring county then summing the weighted income values. While this is the most intuitive way to summaries the neighbors’ values it has one drawback in that polygons along the edges of the study area will base their lagged values on fewer polygons thus potentially over- or under-estimating the true nature of the spatial autocorrelation in the data. For this example, we’ll stick with the style=“W” option for simplicity’s sake but note that other more robust options are available, notably style=“B”.

rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q, style="W", zero.policy = TRUE)

The zero.policy=TRUE option allows for lists of non-neighbors. This should be used with caution since the user may not be aware of missing neighbors in their dataset however, a zero.policy of FALSE would return an error.

The spatial window sum is the counter part of the window average, but without using row-standardized weights.
To add the diagonal element to the neighbour list, we just need to use include.self() from spdep.

wm_qs <- include.self(wm_q)
wm_qs

Next, we will assign binary weights to the neighbour structure that includes the diagonal element.

b_weights <- lapply(wm_qs, function(x) 0*x + 1)
